card.title: How Many Meeting Rooms?
card.sub: Two Pointers Over Starts and Ends · Medium

a1.cap: Given meeting times [start, end], return the minimum number of rooms needed so no two overlapping meetings share a room. A room freed at time t can be reused by a meeting starting at t.
a1.say: Given meeting times start, end, return the minimum number of rooms needed so no two overlapping meetings share a room. A room freed at time t can be reused by a meeting starting at t.

lines: Given meeting times [start, end], return the minimum number of rooms needed so no two overlapping meetings share a room. A room freed at time t can be reused by a meeting starting at t.

a1.cap: For example, with meetings = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]], the answer is 2.
a1.say: For example, with meetings equals 0, 30, 5, 10, 15, 20, the answer is 2.

a1.cap: Sort all start times and, separately, all end times. Walk the starts with one pointer; a second pointer tracks the earliest meeting still running.
If the next meeting starts before that earliest end, we need a new room; otherwise a room frees up and we reuse it.
Let's walk through it with meetings = [[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]].
a1.say: Let's walk through it with meetings equals 0, 30, 5, 10, 15, 20.

a1.cap: A meeting starts at 0 before the earliest one ends (10): open a room. Rooms: 1.
A meeting starts at 5 before the earliest one ends (10): open a room. Rooms: 2.
A meeting ended at 10, so reuse its room for the one at 15.
Time complexity is O(n log n) and extra space is O(n).
a1.say: Time complexity is O of n log n and extra space is O of n.

a1.cap: That's the Two Pointers Over Starts and Ends approach. Now try writing it yourself, in Java or Python!
